list.listitem: Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) can occur in any part of the body, usually at the site of a traumatic injury. C
ACS is an emergency that should be treated with immediate surgical intervention. C
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) is an exertional pain syndrome that usually occurs in the lower extremities. C
CECS can be initially treated with conservative therapy, but ultimately may require surgical intervention for definitive therapy. C
Both ACS and CECS can lead to permanent nervous, vascular, and muscular damage if not treated appropriately. C

background.definition: Compartment syndrome is an acute or chronic clinical condition where elevated pressure within the noncompliant boundaries of a fascial compartment cause ischemic damage to the tissues within that space.

list.listitem: 3.5% of more than 2400 patient visits to a sports medicine center were for compartment syndrome.
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome can limit or end an athlete's or military member's career.
Acute compartment syndrome: trauma, especially fractures and dislocations; inappropriate casting; surgery; acute overuse or abuse of anabolic steroids. Can occur rarely following snake envenomations.
Risk factors for ACS following tibial plateau fracture include male sex, increasing BMI, multiple trauma and Schatzker type IV-VI fractures.
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome: overuse in endurance athletes; mechanism not well understood.
Acute compartment syndrome: Direct blow leads to hematoma formation and edema in fascial compartment, or constrictive cast in an actively swelling extremity, or acute excessive exercise.
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome: Repetitive endurance exercise increases muscle volume and compartment pressures, leading to impaired venous drainage in fascial compartment.

Tibial fractures and tibial fracture repair are risk factors for acute compartment syndrome (ACS). Some experts recommend continuous compartment pressure readings to ensure early diagnosis and surgical management in tibial fracture patients and those who have had surgical fracture repair. C

A retrospective study of 850 patients treated at a single institution for a tibial diaphyseal fracture estimated the sensitivity and specificity of compartment pressure monitoring for ACS to be 94 percent and 98 percent, respectively (LR+ 47, LR- 0.06). B
One study of 200 patients concluded that continuous monitoring is not recommended if patients are alert and adequately observed. B
Traction during repair and immediately after surgery for tibial-shaft intramedullary nailing increases compartment pressures and is not recommended. C
Pain with passive stretch and/or out-of-proportion to injury, paresis, pulselessness, pallor, and paresthesias (5 Ps) are specific but insensitive for acute compartment syndrome (ACS) diagnosis. C
Slit or wick catheter measurement of intracompartmental pressures is the recommended diagnostic test. C
MRI, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), and ultrasound are alternative diagnostic tests but may not be as accurate. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain present at beginning of activity
Weakness or loss of function distal to injury
Swelling distal to injury, venous stasis changes
Weight loss, mass, focal findings on radiography

list.listitem: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, as intracompartmental pressure readings may be inaccurate.

History should focus on the Ps (pain with passive stretch and/or out-of-proportion to injury, paresis, pulselessness, pallor, and paresthesias). These findings are very specific but not very sensitive.
Muscle weakness, pallor, and pulselessness are late findings.
Palpate and inspect for fascial herniations.
The patient usually reports some or all of the above symptoms, occurring during and immediately after exercise and resolving with rest.
Clinical examination alone is not reliable for diagnosis of CECS.
The most commonly involved compartments in CECS are the anterior and deep posterior compartments of the lower legs.
Neurologic findings are specific to the involved anatomical compartment.
Slit or wick catheter intracompartmental pressure measurements are the most widely used tests.
A small study found that MRI and NIRS were moderately accurate; NIRS was more sensitive than MRI.

A retrospective study of 850 patients treated at a single institution for a tibial diaphyseal fracture estimated the sensitivity and specificity of compartment pressure monitoring for ACS to be 94 percent and 98 percent, respectively (LR+ 47, LR- 0.06). B
Another small study showed some accuracy using ultrasound for diagnosis.
A single small study of Tc-99m-tetrofosmin single-photon emission CT demonstrated poor accuracy.
Perform a focused history (assess for the Ps) and physical examination (palpate/inspect for fascial herniations).
Obtain radiographs of affected area to rule out fracture or tumor and consider bone scan or MRI to rule out stress fracture.
If ACS is suspected, perform above steps and consider measurement of intracompartmental pressure.
If CECS suspected, measure intracompartmental pressure before and after exercise, looking for increase in pressure (>30 mm Hg 1 minute after exercise or >15 mm Hg 15 minutes after exercise).
Diagnostic exercise testing should include the same activity as that which caused the patient's original symptoms.
Acute compartment syndrome (ACS): emergent surgical fasciotomy on affected compartment(s). C
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS): relative rest, ice, and elevation immediately postexercise; surgical fasciotomy if conservative therapy does not help. C
NSAIDs or acetaminophen may be used for CECS postexercise, but clinical trial data are lacking.
Fasciotomy with or without partial fasciectomy in affected compartments, emergently in ACS and scheduled in CECS.
Some experts recommend releasing all 4 compartments of the lower extremity in CECS, but clinical trial data to support this recommendation are lacking.
CECS: Avoid activities that cause symptoms.
CECS: Relative rest, ice, and elevation immediately postexercise can decrease swelling and limit ischemia.
ACS and CECS: Compression is not recommended.
ACS: Refer to orthopedic surgeon emergently for immediate surgery.
CECS: Refer for orthopedic surgery if conservative methods have failed and patient desires to continue with activity.
ACS: Delayed treatment can result in arrhythmias, amputation, renal failure from myoglobinuria, and even death. C
CECS: Surgical fasciotomy with partial fasciectomy allows the majority of patients to return to preinjury activities and reduces pain. C
Surgery will likely be required for definitive CECS management.
Postsurgery patients may not be able to return to preinjury level of competition or be completely pain free.
A systematic review of case series of forearm CECS, mostly in motorcycle racers, found rates of return to sports over 90% and return to pre-injury levels in 86%.
